The next pass · step 1 of 3 · waiting for your OK

New music, a story that connects, a star worth catching, and one signal for “tap”

Everything you asked to see before anything is built: the nine songs measured, the story's new flow, the star collection and the camera rise as stills, the new visual language with six freeze-frames, and Emberwick planned on its new song. Nothing here is in the game except the visual language, which is behind a switch so you can try it. The decisions I need are at the end.

1. The music, measured

All nine songs are downloaded from ncs.io and measured. Six have an instrumental on NCS and I used it. Luna, Memory Box and Darkness have no instrumental there; Darkness is sung (She Is Jules), so its voice stays unless you choose otherwise.

How they were measured. Tempo and first beat come from fitting a grid to every drum hit in the whole song. On all nine the tempo is a whole number and drifts less than 2 ms a minute, so a chart stays locked from first bar to last. Sections, drops and beat strength come from loudness and drum patterns, bar by bar. I cannot hear. Everything below is measurement; whether a song feels right for its world is yours to judge. Keys are computed estimates, and I mark the ones I am unsure of.

2. The story, start to finish

Your playtest said the opening was too short to understand and then cut twice: into an upbeat song, and into the map. This is the flow that removes both cuts.

The cold open: the Harmonic Nebula (50 to 55 seconds, new)

TimeYou seeYou hearYou doWritten in the sky (your words)
0:00The Harmonic Nebula alive in gold. Comets pass; everything turns on one pulseHelion's theme begins, clear and warmLong before the stars fell silent, the Harmonic Nebula spun to a single, golden pulse.
0:08Orbin and Helion on one orbit, in stepThe theme, with a soft beatA twin orbit: one tap moves both. About ten taps. It cannot be failedTwo twin sparks of starlight: Orbin and his brother Helion.
0:30At the edge of the gold a constellation goes out. Colour drains inward. Helion drifts off the beat; Orbin's taps still landThe music loses its tempo: it slows, dulls and skipsThree or four more taps, each a little lonelierThen came the Stillness.
0:44The dark takes Helion. Orbin reaches; their hands brushOne held note; everything else goneOne tap: the reach
0:48The shockwave. White, then blackSilence

Three lines of text, all yours. The brothers' own words stay in the memories. A returning player can skip the cold open with one quiet word in the corner; a first launch cannot.

The first stage: The Drifting Edge (your storyboard, now a level of its own)

  • Your storyboard plays exactly as built now, up to the word “tap”. Nothing in it changes.
  • The first tap blooms the world and starts Where We Started, not Emberwick's song. The sad moment and the song that answers it are the same piece of music, so there is no jolt.
  • Orbin learns on this planetoid, on that one song: first only Star-Nodes; then the hop to the next ring; then one hold. Nothing else. The first sixteen beats cannot be failed, as now.
  • The stage ends on the song's last big hit: the planetoid's own star rises and Orbin catches it. The first star.

The camera rise: from the planetoid to the galaxy map, in one move

The camera lifts from where Orbin stands. The planetoid stays in the picture and becomes the Landing at the bottom of the map; the sleeping worlds drift in; the guardian and the three rings settle at the top with Helion's signal pulsing behind them. About six seconds. The song fades under the Landing's theme during the move. It is one painting seen from further and further away, so there is no screen change to hide.

3. The star collection

  • Our own star. Not a five-pointed character: a Star-Node's star, risen. A small hot heart with eight uneven rays and one thin orbit tilted round it in the world's colour, like the one round Orbin's head. Every world's star has its own orbit colour.
  • The sting. A short rising flourish of Helion's theme on a music box over one warm chord, written in each song's key and timed to start on the catch. I make it by synthesis and cannot hear it; you judge it in the listening room before it goes in.
  • The camera turn is one slow quarter-turn of the sky round Orbin during the burst, eased in and out. It is painted layers moving at different speeds, not a 3D camera.
  • Replays get the quick version: the star is already in the sky, so a small echo of it rises, Orbin touches it, and the results line is written. No flight home.
  • The count. The star you catch is the world's main star. The other four per world (shards in one flight, daredevil, every node on the beat, the far side) stay as they are, smaller.

4. The Landing as a resting place

Only the mood is taken from your reference: nothing in it is reproduced, and it stays in the Afterglow hand, not pixel art. Storyboard quality here; the finished painting is made in step 2.

  • Two lights. Cool starlight from one pale cluster high in the sky lies over everything. The fire is the only warm thing in the picture, and everything near it is lit by it. Helion's signal on the horizon is the same warm colour, kept small and far: the fire is where you are, the signal is where you are going.
  • The palette is deep blues, teals and night greens, with that one warm accent.
  • Five layers, each hazier and cooler: flowers and grass; Orbin and the fire; the Sleeper; mist; the horizon with the guardian, the three rings and the signal. They slide past each other gently whenever the camera moves.
  • The fire is made of the stars he has brought home. A tiny ember on the first visit. Each star sits small in its heart, in its own world's colour, and the fire is larger and warmer for every one. Flowers and grass come back round it, nearest first.
  • The Sleeper: the planetoid itself. An old being of stone, asleep since before the Stillness. The hill behind the fire is its bowed head and shoulder; the three great fingers of rock round the fire are its hand, cupped. It has no face: only one long closed seam of soft light where an eye would be, which opens a little with every star. It never speaks. It is not a tree, and it is nothing like the reference's.
  • Quiet motion: sparks rising, motes drifting, mist sliding, flowers swaying. Nothing loud.
  • After each star the flight home ends with a short quiet beat here (about three seconds: Orbin settles, the new star drops into the fire, the fire answers) before the map can be used. Replays skip it.
  • The sound is fire crackle and night air with a soft music-box version of Helion's theme, crossfading in and out of the levels. I synthesise all three and cannot hear them: you judge them in the listening room.
  • The title can be this same scene: Orbin asleep by the fire, the name written in the sky above the horizon, and the first tap wakes him and the camera rises to the map. On a first launch the cold open still comes first.

How this fits the map: the Landing is the bottom of the same painting the camera rises out of. Tapping the Landing on the map brings the camera back down to the fire, where its places are (the still pool, the rim, settings by the fire).

5. One visual language

  • One signal: a gold ring that closes on a star and touches its edge on the beat. Every tap in the game wears it: a node on the path, an orb in the air, a pad, a gate, the drop's great node. No ring, no tap.
  • Gold is the tap's alone. Danger stays vermilion. A hold is a calm blue ribbon. Everything else (the path, rings, particles, Orbin's trail, the core) is in quiet blues that cannot be mistaken for it.
  • Only the next two taps are lit. Nodes after them are small unlit stones until their turn. A node goes dark again the moment it is tapped.
  • Optional gold notes: I recommend removing them as separate targets. Flow is then earned by tapping the nodes themselves on the beat, which is what you are already doing. It removes the single biggest source of “is that one mine?”. The alternative (keeping them but drawing them unmistakably different) still puts a second kind of target on the course.
  • The star stretch is a quiet dotted line well outside the path, with a small star beside it. Nothing extra on the course.
  • At the drop the spectacle goes into the sky and the inhabitant, behind the course. The number of marks does not rise.

You can try it now on the current levels: add ?look=2 to the address (with ?fresh: ?fresh&look=2). It is switched off by default until you approve it.

What I see in them, honestly. The gold rings do single out the taps, and no frame has more than two. But these frames are on the old chart, and three things in them still compete with the signal: the form gates with their labels (METEOR, ORB), the violet walls, and the red closed rings, sometimes several at once. The re-chart removes most of them (section 7: one main idea per world, a form for a whole phrase), and the gates that remain are redrawn in the quiet family in step 2. How busy it is. About a hundred taps in 79 seconds. Never faster than one every 0.6 s, except the double strike, which is two taps a fifth of a second apart. With the new look that is at most two lit taps on screen at any time.

Two things I am changing from the last build, unless you say no. Ossa's line moves from the end of the level to the moment the gift is given (bar 8), because that is where it now means something. And the gift is given inside the level, at the song's own turn, instead of in a scene after it.

What I am unsure of. The stab and kick positions are detected, not heard: I check each against the waveform while charting, and your ear is the last check. The double strike may be too sharp for a first world; if it is in your playtest, it moves to the far side and the drop's second half keeps single walls with a new phrasing.

8. Smooth, and fun to touch (built in step 2)

  • The picture is drawn between simulation steps (interpolated), the camera follows on eased springs, and a form change morphs over about 150 ms instead of popping.
  • Orbin gets anticipation before a hop, squash on landing, stretch at speed and a small follow-through, on weighted arcs.
  • Every tap answers in the frame it lands: a pitched note from the song's key, the node's star bursting, the ring snapping shut. An early or late tap shows a small tick before or after the node, with no penalty beyond flow.
  • Frame times are logged through the busiest drop and reported with the worst frame. If anything has to give, effects go before smoothness. I can measure this on a slowed processor; only you can measure it on your iPhone.

9. Credits

In step 2 the credits change to: Music provided by NoCopyrightSounds (ncs.io). Private test build. with every new track and its artists listed. The line about a game licence is removed until you confirm one.

10. Decisions for you

  1. Gold belongs to the tap. Orbin is gold too, so in play I draw him paler with a short dim trail (as in the freeze-frames). My recommendation: keep gold for the tap. The alternative is a different colour for the tap and gold left to Orbin.
  2. Optional gold notes go. Flow is earned by tapping the nodes themselves on the beat. My recommendation: remove them.
  3. Helion's theme. Memory Box plays the five memories. For the cold open, the star's sting and the fire, I recommend keeping the music-box melody I wrote, retuned to sit with Memory Box (F minor): the cold open has to slow it, dull it and make it skip, and I should not do that to someone else's recording. The alternative is the cold open on Memory Box's own quiet opening, unaltered, with the Stillness shown in the picture only.
  4. The Sleeper as the Landing's old presence: yes, no, or change it?
  5. The title as the Landing, Orbin asleep by the fire and waking on the first tap. My recommendation: yes.
  6. The planetoid's own star counts. It is the first star in the fire and in the count, so World 1 holds 21. The gate before the guardian stays where you set it. My recommendation: yes.
  7. Darkness is sung. NCS has no instrumental of it. Keep the voice in the ambush, or should I look for another track?
